daśāpavitra
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices were very common during the early phase of हिन्दुइस्म्. Among the various yāgas or sacrifices, the Somayāgas were performed with the सोम juice, the सोम plant being a special kind of creeper. This creeper had to be crushed for extracting the juice and then filtered. The strainer was the दशापवित्र and the vessel into which the juice would get collected, the द्रोणकलश.
The दशापवित्र was made of the wool cut from a living ram, the wool being white. The dimensions had to conform to the directions given in the श्रौतसूत्रस्.

daśatāla
(‘ten spans’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism allows the worship of icons or images of deities, not only as their symbolical representations but as the deities themselves, when imbued with their subtle presence through appropriate rites such as आवाहन (inviting) and प्राणप्रतिष्ठा (infusing life).
Such images which are generally installed in temples for public worship are to be prepared strictly according to the principles of मूर्तिशिल्पशास्त्र or icono-graphy. The basic unit of length used in the sculpturing of images is called ‘tāla’ (or span). It is the measurement of the palm of the hand (from the tip of the middle finger to the wrist) and is equal to the length of the face (from the top of the forehead to the bottom of the chin). This ताल is again divided into 12 equal parts, each part being designated as ‘aṅgula’.
While sculpturing the images, standards are prescribed, based on this ताल (and the aṅgulas). Hence this system is called the ‘tālamāna’ paddhati or system.
If an image is to be ‘daśatāla,’ it simply means that the total height from the bottom of the feet (in the standing posture) to the top of the head should be ten tālas.
The दशताल measurement is divided into three varieties: uttama (superior), madhyama (middling) and adhama (inferior). The proportions are 124, 120, and 116 aṅgulas respectively.
The दशताल is the most preferred scale for making the images of the major deities and their female counter parts. It is prescribed for the icons that are worshiped for getting various benefits.
See also MŪRTIŚILPAŚĀSTRA.

Dāśarājña
(‘[the battle of] the ten kings’)
------------------------------------------
See SUDĀSA.

Dasyus
(‘those who destroy others’)
------------------------------------------
The words ‘Ārya’ and ‘Dasyu’ are found in the Ṛgveda itself (vide 1.34.7; 1.100.18; 1.51.8; 1.117.21). The word ‘Dasyu’ has been used there in several senses such as: super-human enemies, human foes, aborigines and so on. Some of the words used to describe them give us the impression that they were flat-nosed, ugly and unclean persons who did not perform the sacrificial rites (of the आर्यन्स्), hated the gods and were addicted to strange practices.
Cumuri, Śambara and Śuṣṇa are some of the names of the well-known दस्युस् mentioned in the वेदस्.
They were probably primitive settlers of the regions conquered by the आर्यन्स्. Or, they might have been the renegades in the Āryan society who were cultural outcastes. In later literature the word refers to criminals committing atrocities on peace-loving people.
Indra, the lord of the gods, is sometimes referred to as ‘dasyuhatya’ (one who destroys the दस्युस्).
The Iranian terms ‘daṅhu’ and ‘daqyn’ are similar to the word ‘Dasyu’ and indicate a country inhabited by hostile people.

dāsa and dāsī
(‘a [paid] servant or servant-maid’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘dāsa’ occurs in the Ṛgveda (5.34.6; 6.22.10) many times and refers to the enemies of the Vedic people. Since these dāsas were, in many cases, reduced to स्लवेर्य्, the term has been used in the sense of a ‘slave’ also. (See SLAVERY.)
In later literature, the word refers to a paid servant.
While naming a person, this word was used as a suffix for persons belonging to the śūdra caste.
In the devotional literature, this expression has been widely used to indicate a devotee as a servant of God or as a servant of the devotees of God. For instance: रामदास, Kṛṣṇadāsa, चण्डी-dāsa and so on.

Daśaśāntis
(‘ten propitiatory hymns’)
------------------------------------------
Śāntimantras are propitiatory Vedic chants or hymns used on several occasions including during Vedic studies.
Ten such शान्तिमन्त्रस् are sometimes grouped together and are technically designated as ‘Daśaśāntayaḥ’.
The following are those listed under it:
bhadraṁ karṇebhiḥ....
namo brahmaṇe....
namo vāce....
śaṁ no vātaḥ pavatām....
saṁ tvā siñcāmi....
śaṁ no mitraḥ....
tac-chaṁyorāvṛṇīmahe....
saha nāvavatu....
vāṅ me manasi....
pūrṇamadaḥ....
All these, except the fourth and the fifth, have been dealt with under ‘Śāntimantras’. (See ŚĀNTIMANTRAS.)
The fifth mantra—saṁ tvā siñcāmi....—is actually from the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (1.6.1). It is used to address the ghee that has been spilled over in a sacrifice. Simultaneously a wish is expressed to obtain longevity and sons as also wealth.
Here it is listed as a śānti मन्त्र.
The fourth मन्त्र is a very long passage with verses selected from various sections of the वेदस्. The ideas contained in it are also many and varied.
The Daśaśāntis are often chanted in full on special occasions involving important rituals.
See also ŚĀNTIMANTRAS.

Dāsabodha
(‘[spiritual and philosophical] wisdom [as taught by Samartha] रामदास’)
------------------------------------------
Samartha Rāmadās (A.
-1681) was a great saint of Maharashtra. He was the गुरु (preceptor and guide) of Chatrapati Śivājī (A.

-1680). It was he who was primarily responsible for the rejuvenation of Hindu religion and society by inspiring Śivājī.
He has left behind him two immortal works both in Marāṭhi: Manāce Śloka and Dāsabodha.
The work Dāsabodha comprises twenty daśakas or decads. Each of these daśakas consists of ten long sections called samāsas. The samāsas again, have a number of ovīs or metrical stanzas, their total number being 7756.
The contents in brief may be given as follows:
Daśaka-1 (326 stanzas)
prayers to गणेश, सरस्वती, गुरु and saints; greatness and usefulness of human birth.
Daśaka-2 (470 stanzas)
descriptions of various types of persons, from fools to wise persons; the three guṇas सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्; characte-ristics of a good and holy person.
Daśaka-3 (581 stanzas)
various evils in worldly life; tāpatrayas or three kinds of sufferings; death and detachment.
Daśaka-4 (295 stanzas)
navavidha भक्ति (nine modes of devotion); four kinds of मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्.
Daśaka-5 (573 stanzas)
characteristics of a good गुरु (spiritual teacher) and of a good शिष्य or disciple; different kinds of teachings on sādhanā (spiritual practice); signs of a siddha or a perfected being.
Daśaka-6 (415 stanzas)
on ब्रह्मन्, māyā and सृष्टि or च्रेअतिओन्; worship of God with form; denial of this world which is seen but does not really exist; indescribable nature of ब्रह्मन्.
Daśaka-7 (564 stanzas)
fourteen kinds of ब्रह्मन्; offsetting the effects of द्वैत or sense of duality; on śravaṇa (listening to the Vedāntic truths); death and jīvanmukta (one who is liberated even while living).
Daśaka-8 (644 stanzas)
on God; various kinds of doubts; the pañcamahābhūtas (the five elements); on मोक्ष (liberation) and the perfected being.
Daśaka-9 (427 stanzas)
various kinds of doubts and their answers; description of the inner state of a man of knowledge.
Daśaka-10 (354 stanzas)
the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् in all, is one and the same; च्रेअतिओन् and dissolution; प्रकृति (nature) and पुरुष (soul).
Daśaka-11 (287 stanzas)
on च्रेअतिओन् and dissolution of the world; four kinds of manifestations of God; how a sādhaka (spiritual aspirant) should lead his life; behaviour of a true leader of a society; nature of the Self within.
Daśaka-12 (294 stanzas)
on devotion; विवेक (discrimination) and वैराग्य (renunciation); need for self-effort; how to become great.
Daśaka-13 (300 stanzas)
philosophical truths through a story; on God the creator, various opinions; need to protect the purity of one’s मिन्द्.
Daśaka-14 (406 verses)
desirelessness necessary; a sādhaka (aspirant) should live by भिक्षा (begging); efficacy of singing God’s names; greatness of a householder’s life and the need to keep it pure; remember God constantly.
Daśaka-15 (337 stanzas)
how to live in this world, in peace and harmony with others; knowledge makes one superior to others; ब्रह्मन् as the origin of the world; all activities of प्रकृति (nature) and पुरुष (individual सोउल्) are transient; interpretation of the महावाक्यस् of the उपनिषद्स् (like tat-tvam-asi).
Daśaka-16 (302 verses)
hymns devoted to वाल्मीकि, सूर्य (sun-god) and the five elements like the earth and water; on the आत्मन् or the Self; various types of upāsanā or meditation.
Daśaka-17 (299 stanzas)
Supreme God (Jagadīśvara) manifests himself as various souls; शिव and शक्ति are at the root of all beings, male and female; doubts are obstacles in the path of understanding Vedāntic truths; explanation of ajapājapa (process of breathing associated with the repetition of the मन्त्र so’ham); four kinds of bodies.
Daśaka-18 (288 stanzas)
This section deals with miscellaneous topics like various gods—Gaṇapati, ब्रह्मा, वेङ्कटेश, राम, कृष्ण and so on—as different manifestations of the Antarātman (the आत्मन् inside), company of jñānis (persons of spiritual wisdom), importance of human body in the path of spiritual progress and so on.
Daśaka-19 (285 stanzas)
on handwriting and scholarship; condemnation of laziness; signs of a wise person; methods of giving good advice; efficiency in work and management.
Daśaka-20 (308 stanzas)
discussion about pūrṇa and apūrṇa (what is complete and what is incomplete); the three guṇas; upāsanā or meditation on God with form; interesting details about 84 lakhs of species of living beings; on the आत्मन्; body compared to a field; on परब्रह्मन् (the Absolute).
The work is extremely popular especially in Maharashtra.
A ceremonial recitation and discourses on it are considered as a religious and meritorious act.
See also RĀMADĀSA (SAMARTHA).

Daśaratha
(‘One [who could drive his] chariot [in] ten [directions]’)
------------------------------------------
Ancient Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य् traces all the kings of Bharatavarṣa (India) to two primeval races: The Sūryavaṁśa and the चन्द्रवṁश. Since इक्ष्वाकु and रघु were the most outstanding emperors of the Sūryavaṁśa, the race has also been known by their names as Ikṣvākuvaṁśa or Raghuvaṁśa. But, the very best of all the kings of this race was राम or Śrī राम, considered and worshipped as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु himself. दशरथ was the ड़थेर् of this राम and the son of another great king of this lineage, Aja.
Though the impression created by the Ayodhyākāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि is that दशरथ was a weak king, a prisoner of his infatuation for his wife कैकेयी and a doting ड़थेर्, he was actually a great hero and a good ruler in his younger days. The very word ‘Daśaratha’ which means ‘one who could drive his रथ or chariot in daśa or ten directions’, is proof enough of his valour.
He was the king of कोसल with its capital at अयोध्या. He had three queens—Kausalyā, सुमित्रा, and Kaikeyī—who were the daughters of the kings Bhānumanta, शूरसेन and अश्वपति Kekaya respectively. A cabinet of eight distinguished ministers, under the able guidance of सुमन्त्र, assisted him in administration.
He had a daughter called Śāntādevī, but no male issues, Śāntādevi had been adopted by the king रोमपाद as his daughter and had been married to the sage ऋष्यशृङ्ग.
On the advice of the royal preceptor वसिष्ठ, दशरथ performed the पुत्र-kāmeṣṭi sacrifice with ऋष्यशृङ्ग as the head-priest and was blessed with four sons. राम (from कौसल्या), भरत (from कैकेयी), लक्ष्मण and शत्रुघ्न (from सुमित्रा).
The four princes grew up into fine young men under the able tutelage of the highly competent sage वसिष्ठ.
Once, the sage विश्वामित्र arrived at the court of दशरथ and requested him to send राम and लक्ष्मण with him to guard the sacrifice he was conducting, against the ruinous attacks of the demons Mārīca and Subāhu. Though दशरथ was at first unwilling, he later on acceded to the request of the sage (on the intervention of वसिष्ठ, who knew better) and sent his two sons.
After some heroic exploits and excellent training in the arts of war and peace under विश्वामित्र, the youths arrived at the capital मिथिला of the king जनक. When the Śivadhanus, the mythical bow of god शिव, was broken by राम, to win the hand of princess सीता, जनक’s daughter, दशरथ arrived soon at मिथिला with his entourage and took part in the मर्रिअगे of राम and सीता, and also of the other three princes with suitable brides.
As he was getting old, he decided to instal राम as the Yuvarāja (crown-prince). When the preparations were in an advanced stage, कैकेयी, under the wicked spell of her malicious maid Mantharā, demanded the fulfilment of the two boons दशरथ had given her long back. They were: making her son भरत the king and banishing राम to the forest for fourteen years. Unable, either to change her मिन्द् or to accede to her demand, the mortally shocked दशरथ passed away. Meanwhile राम, along with his wife सीता and brother लक्ष्मण had already left for the forest as per कैकेयी’s words, conveying the ‘order’ of the king and ड़थेर् दशरथ.
Daśaratha is said to have met this tragic end due to the curse of a sage-couple whose only son he had killed by mistake, long back, in his youth.
As per the description of the Rāmāyaṇa दशरथ was a good and noble king who had ruled his kingdom righteously.
See also RĀMĀYAṆA.

Daśamahāvidyās
(‘ten great representa-tions of knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
Ten aspects of शक्ति are sometimes described in tāntric works. They are termed ‘Daśamahāvidyā’s. These are the representations of transcendental know-ledge and power, the sources of all that is to be known.
The first is Kālī, the goddess of time, that destroys everything. तारा, the second, is the power of the golden embryo (Hiraṇya-garbha) from which the universe evolves. She also stands for void or the boundless space. The third is षोडशी. The word literally means ‘one who is sixteen years old.’ She is the personification of fullness, of perfection. भुवनेश्वरी, the fourth विद्या, represents the forces of the material world, whereas भैरवी the fifth, stands for desires and temptations leading to destruction and death. Then comes छिन्नमस्ता, the naked deity holding her own severed head in hand and drinking her own blood! She simply represents the continued state of self-sustenance of the created world in which are seen continuous self-destruction and self-renewal, in a cyclic order. Dhūmāvatī, the seventh, personifies the destruction of the world by fire, when only smoke (Dhūma) from its ashes remains. She is sometimes identified with अलक्ष्मी or Jyeṣṭhādevī. The eighth विद्या, Bagalā, is a crane-headed goddess, and represents the ugly side of living creatures like jealousy, hatred and cruelty. Mātaṅgī, the ninth, is the embodiment of the power of domination. The tenth and the last, Kamalā, is the pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the Self, bestowing boons and allaying the fears of the supplicants. She is identified with लक्ष्मी, the goddess of fortune.

Daśarathajātaka
------------------------------------------
Over the centuries, the story of Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, has given rise to many other literary works which are faithful adaptations of the original, or, are at variance with it. The Daśarathajātaka, numbered as 461 in the जातक Tales series, is one such, belonging to the latter group. In this जातक, the main story of the Rāmāyaṇa has been retold in a startlingly distorted form.
Daśaratha was the king of वाराणसी. Rāmapaṇḍita, Lakṣmaṇakumāra and सीता-देवी were his children by his chief queen. Bharatakumāra was the son of his second wife who became the chief queen after the death of the first. At her behest, to fulfil a boon he had promised earlier he was forced to exile the first three children for 14 years and hand over the kingdom to her son Bharatakumāra. Meanwhile he died. When Rāmapaṇḍita returned after the period of exile was over, he became the king.
It is strange that the जातक tale narrates राम as having married सीता who was his own sister!
The view that the Daśarathajātaka must have been based on a much older राम story has been thoroughly discounted by scholars of repute, who have shown that the case may just be the reverse!
See also RĀMĀYAṆA.

dāsakūṭa
(‘an assembly of the servants [of God]’)
------------------------------------------
In the religio-philosophical literature of हिन्दुइस्म् both भक्ति (devotion) and ज्ञान (knowledge) have been given equal prominence. The various teachers of भक्ति, over the centuries, gave the common masses a simple philosophy of life to live by. This they did through their teachings, mostly in the form of devotional songs.
The tradition of devotion with its popular religion and एथिच्स्, was originated in North India by the musician-saints like Tulasīdās (A.
-1547) and others. In Maharashtra, it was Sant Jñāneśvar (13th cent. A. D.), Ekanāth (A.
-1681) and a host of others who did the same. In Bengal, श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य (A.

?) were the important teachers.
In South India, the आऌवार्स् (7th to 9th centuries A. D.) and Nāyanmārs (7th and 8th centuries A. D.) spread the cult of भक्ति in the Tamil country. The शिव-śaraṇas (12th cent. A. D.) and the Haridāsas (15th cent. A. D.) were the pioneers of the भक्ति movement in Karnataka.
The Haridāsa movement comprised two parallel but closely knit units, generally called the ‘Vyāsakūṭa’ and the ‘Dāsakūṭa’. The former was nourished by the saṁnyāsins of the Mādhva school like Śrīpādarāya (15th cent. A. D.) and व्यास-rāya (A.
-1539) whereas the latter was sustained by पुरन्दरदास (A.

-1755) and other householder-devotees of the same school.
Though the Vyāsakūṭa derived its name from Vyāsarāya (also known as व्यासतीर्थ) who was responsible for the phenomenal growth of both the units, it was Śrīpādarāya who was the pioneer of both.
The saṁnyāsin teachers were great scholars both in Sanskrit and in Kannaḍa (the vernacular of Karnataka). They composed scholarly works in the former and popular devotional songs in the latter. The Haridāsas—though quite a few of them also were great scholars—concentrated on spreading the cult of devotion and the द्वैत Vedānta of मध्वाचार्य (A.

-1276) as also simple ethical principles through their songs which became very popular over the centuries.
Apart from पुरन्दरदास and विजयदास, Gopāladāsa (A.

-1809) too have contributed profusely to the Haridāsa literature.
Some of the other Haridāsas who contributed significantly to the दासकूट and the भक्ति movement are: वैकुण्ठ-dāsa, Prasanna-Veṅkaṭadāsa, Timmaṇṇa-dāsa, Mohanadāsa, Heḷavanakaṭṭe Giri-yamma (a lady-saint), Kallūru Subbaṇṇa-dāsa, Aijīdāsa and so on.
The Vijayanagara city and the Raichur district of Karnataka were the main centres of origin and activities of these Haridāsas.
The compositions of these Haridāsas are legion. Their chief characteristic is simplicity. They express the profound truths of Vedānta in a simple language and urge the people to lead a God-centred life even while discharging one’s normal duties in the world. The topics generally dealt with are: description of God’s form and beauty (almost always as विष्णु or कृष्ण), childhood pranks of कृष्ण, various devotional practices like repetition of the divine name or singing the glories of God, moral principles like सत्य (truth) and धर्म (righteous living), evil nature of the evil ones (in order to avoid such conduct), some paurāṇic stories as also autobiographical references, activism as well as dependence on God and a host of other miscellaneous subjects.
The contribution of the दासकूट to Hindu religion and culture through the life and literature of the various Haridāsas is considerable.

Dasarā
(‘[festival of] ten days’)
------------------------------------------
Festivals and sacred days, which are the popular manifestations of any religion, are legion in हिन्दुइस्म्.
Dasarā Procession at MysoreOne of the major festivals observed throughout India is the दसरा festival. It is celebrated from the Āśvayuja śukla pratipad to the daśamī (the bright half of the month Āśvayuja or Āśvina, generally falling in September-October), for nine days (Navarātri, festival of nine nights) or ten days (dasarā = daśa + ahar = ten days). This festival takes many forms. In Bengal, Bihar and Orissa it is celebrated as the दुर्गापूजा, worship of the Divine मोथेर् दुर्गा, usually in a clay image. In Uttar Pradesh and some other northern States it is observed as रामलीला, a re-enactment of the राम story.
In Karnataka, it is a multifestival, comprising सरस्वतीपूजा on the saptamī, दुर्गापूजा on the aṣṭamī and Āyudhapūjā (worship of weapons and implements) on the navamī days.
The tenth day known as विजय-daśamī, again, is observed as the day for immersion of the दुर्गा images after the दुर्गापूजा, wherever it is observed.
Where रामलीला is enacted, विजय-daśamī is celebrated as the day of victory of राम over रावण, the demon-king.
It is also the day on which kings used to start on expeditions of victory or conquests for expansion. Worship of the śamīvṛkṣa (Prosopis spicigera) and the royal weapons like the sword, as also the royal horse and the elephant were part of the विजयदशमी festival.
As per the account of various foreign travellers like Abdur Razak (A.

), the दसरा was being celebrated in all pomp and glory as a State festival with the king being given the prime place, in Vijayanagara, the capital of the Vijayanagara empire. After the fall of the empire, it was taken up by the kings of Mysore State, and celebrated in a grand manner. The celebrations are continued even now, though as a peoples’ festival.
See also DURGĀPŪJĀ, RĀMALĪLĀ and VIJAYADAŚAMĪ.

Daśanāmīs
(‘those [belonging to the order] of ten names’)
------------------------------------------
Saṁnyāsa or मोनस्तिचिस्म् is a very ancient institution. The धर्मशास्त्रस् list it as the fourth and last stage in a man’s life. (See ĀŚRAMA for details.)
Organised मोनस्तिचिस्म् into a regular Order (in हिन्दुइस्म्)—though common among the Buddhists—can be attributed to शङ्कर’s (A.

daśahotāraḥ
(‘ten होतृ priests’)
------------------------------------------
The religion of the Vedic आर्यन्स् comprised mostly of the performance of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्. Out of these, अग्न्याधेय or अग्न्याधान was a primary rite meant for generating the Vedic fires like the गार्हपत्य. These fires had to be maintained for life and all other sacrifices had to be performed only in them.
The ‘daśahotāraḥ’ is actually a formula of ten sentences taken from the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (3.1). These mantras have to be repeated when the upper अरणि is placed on the lower one before churning, for generating the fire.
These ten short sentences (oṁ cittiḥ sruk; cittam ājyam; vāg vediḥ and so on) actually identify ten different parts of the human body with ten things connected with the sacrifice.

Daśāvatāras
(‘ten incarnations [of Lord विष्णु]’)
------------------------------------------
To ward off the extraordinary perils to which mankind is prone—may be the visitations from the demons, may be from the human malefactors—and to preserve the socio-ethical order, Lord विष्णु whose duty it is to preserve this world, often incarnates himself. Though such incarnations are popularly considered to be ten, there is no limit to their number. Nor are there any restrictions regarding the time and place of their appearance. Whenever धर्म declines and अधर्म prospers he bodies himself forth to restore the balance in the world.
In the मत्स्यावतार (Fish-इन्चर्नतिओन्), the Lord is said to have saved मनु (the progenitor of mankind) and the सप्तर्षिस् (the seven sages, मिन्द्-born sons of ब्रह्मा) along with their wives during the deluge. The world was repopulated through them later on.
Lord विष्णु incarnated himself as the कूर्म (the Tortoise) in order to support the mount मन्दर which started sinking during the churning of the ocean (samudra-mathana). The gods and demons had jointly undertaken this adventure to get अमृत (nectar) from the ocean.
Next in the series is the Varāhāva-tāra (Boar-इन्चर्नतिओन्) in which the Lord killed the demon हिरण्याक्ष and lifted the earth out of the flood waters in which it had been submerged. This may be a symbolic representation of the extrication of the world from the deluge of sin by the power of the Supreme Being.
When प्रह्लाद, the great devotee of विष्णु was being severely tortured by his ड़थेर्, the demon हिरण्यकशिपु, (who was a non-believer in the existence of an omnipresent and omnipotent God), नरसिṁह (Man-lion) appeared emerging out of the pillar shown by him and killed him. Being a combination of man (the best of higher creatures) and lion (the best of lower creatures) नरसिṁह represents the best of creations. Incidentally this also proves the omnipresence of God. नरसिṁह is especially the embodiment of valour which is a divine attribute and hence worshipped by rulers and warriors. His मन्त्र is said to be very powerful, capable of destroying enemies and exorcising evil.
When बलि, the grandson of प्रह्लाद, conquered the three worlds, इन्द्र was deprived of his heavenly kingdom. At the request of अदिति, the मोथेर् of इन्द्र, Lord विष्णु incarnated as वामन (the Dwarf), a young ब्राह्मण boy, and approached बलि who was known for his munificence, for a gift of land that could be covered by three steps. With the first and the second he covered the earth and हेअवेन्, and with the third, he pushed down बलि to the netherworld. Hence he is also known as त्रिविक्रम, one who encompassed the world with three big steps.
This myth teaches us that since even God had to resort to the dwarf’s form while begging, one who begs makes himself small! Secondly, a true ब्राह्मण can conquer the three worlds by the power of the spirit. These five avatāras have been referred to in the various sections of the वेदस्.
The next five incarnations are in the human form.
Paraśurāma (Rāma with the battle-axe) is the sixth अवतार. Born as the son of the sage-couple, जमदग्नि and रेणुका, he exterminated the tyrannical among the Kṣattriyas led by Kārtavīrya, who were oppressing the people. Whether this story has any historical basis and represents the struggle for supremacy between the ब्राह्मणस् and kṣattriyas, it is difficult to say.
Śrī राम, the next इन्चर्नतिओन्, met परशुराम and absorbed his power into himself. Hence the latter is sometimes considered as आवेशावतार, an इन्चर्नतिओन् by the temporary possession of विष्णु’s powers.
Śrī राम, one of the two most popular incarnations of the Lord विष्णु, comes next in the series. His story is too well-known to need any repetition. He typifies the ideal man. His story, the Rāmāyaṇa has now become an immortal epic. His name is known as the ‘tāraka-मन्त्र,’ the मन्त्र that takes one across the ocean of transmigration.
Balarāma, राम, the strong, the elder brother of Śrī कृष्ण is the eighth इन्चर्नतिओन्. His many adventures include the slaying of the ape Dvivida and the demon Dhenuka, shaking the ramparts of Hastināvati (the capital city of the Pāṇḍavas) and dragging the river यमुना out of its course. The story that the serpent शेष issued forth from his mouth at the time of his death gives credence to the belief that he was the इन्चर्नतिओन् of शेष. Some scholars, basing their conjecture on the weapon of बलराम (the hala or plough), opine that he was an agricultural hero raised to the status of an अवतार in course of time.
Śrī कृष्ण, the ninth इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु is, perhaps, the most popular, so much so, that he is considered Pūrṇāva-tāra (the इन्चर्नतिओन् in toto) and all other deities are regarded as his manifestations. His story and his exploits are too numerous and too well-known to be mentioned here. To the average Hindu, he is the supreme statesman, warrior, hero, philosopher and teacher, nay, God himself. He is the great expounder of the ‘Song Celestial,’ the Bhagavadgītā.
The tenth अवतार कल्कि, is yet to come. He will descend upon the earth at the end of the present age (Kali Yuga). Riding on the back of a white horse, with a drawn sword, he will destroy the enemies of धर्म and re-establish it in all its glory.
This list of the ten avatāras of Lord विष्णु is by no means the standard one accepted by all. Taking Śrī कृष्ण as विष्णु Himself, he is not included in some lists. His place is taken over by बुद्ध. In some other lists, बुद्ध replaces बलराम. Iconographically speaking, बुद्ध seems to have disappeared from such lists only after the 15th century.
Strangely enough, the purpose of the बुद्ध-इन्चर्नतिओन् was to mislead men of low birth and genius, who had become too proficient in the sacred lore and were a threat to the supremacy of the gods! This looks more like a joke than a serious proposition. It is obvious that the Hindus sealed the fate of बुद्धिस्म् in this country by absorbing बुद्ध into the pantheon of the avatāras.
Haṁsa, सात्वत, यज्ञ, दत्तात्रेय, वेदव्यास are some of the avatāras included in other lists, keeping the total as ten only. The number, however, rises sometimes to as high as twentythree.

Daśaharā
(‘destroyer of ten [sins]’)
------------------------------------------
Festivals and sacred days have a very important part to play in popular हिन्दुइस्म्. They often act as a catalytic agent to integrate the various sections of the Hindu society.
One of the minor festivals, observed mostly in North India and also on the banks of the big rivers like Kṛṣṇā, गोदावरी and नर्मदा, is the दशहरा (also called गङ्गा-दशहरा). It occurs on the tenth day of the bright fortnight (śukla-daśamī) of the month of Jyeṣṭha (May-June). The river गङ्गा is believed to have descended to the earth on this day. If the day happens to be a Tuesday or a Wednesday it is considered even more auspicious. A bath in the river गङ्गा, especially at the Daśāśvamedha-ghāṭ of वाराणसी or काशी (in Uttar Pradesh) on this day is said to destroy ten kinds of sins associated with the body, speech and मिन्द्. The bath should be followed by worship of the prescribed deity and giving gifts to worthy persons.
